description: Parser theory decomposed. LL(k) vs LR(k) vs LALR vs SLR vs GLR vs PEG. Predictive parsing, shift-reduce, conflict resolution, error recovery. The grammar transformations (left-recursion elimination, left-factoring) that bridge human-readable grammars to parsable ones. Pratt parsing for operator precedence.

sub_mechanisms.name: FIRST_set
sub_mechanisms.definition: For grammar symbol α: set of terminals that can start a string derived from α. Used in LL parsing.
sub_mechanisms.why: Lets the predictive parser pick the right production with k tokens of lookahead. FIRST(α) ∩ FIRST(β) = ∅ for two productions A → α | β means LL(1) parsing is unambiguous.

sub_mechanisms.name: FOLLOW_set
sub_mechanisms.definition: For non-terminal A: set of terminals that can appear immediately after A in some derivation. Used in LL parsing for ε-productions.
sub_mechanisms.why: When A can derive ε, parser uses FOLLOW(A) to decide whether to expand A or skip it. Compatibility condition: FIRST(α) ∩ FOLLOW(A) = ∅ for A → α | ε.

sub_mechanisms.name: LL1_parsing_table
sub_mechanisms.definition: Two-dimensional table M[non-terminal][terminal] = production to use. Indexed by current non-terminal + next input token.
sub_mechanisms.why: O(1) per parse step. Compact (sparse) for typical grammars. The mechanical core of LL(1) parsing — table-driven parser is essentially a stack + table lookup.

sub_mechanisms.name: left_recursion_elimination
sub_mechanisms.definition: Transform A → A α | β (left-recursive) into A → β A'; A' → α A' | ε (right-recursive). Required for LL parsing.
sub_mechanisms.why: LL parsers infinite-loop on direct left recursion. Standard transformation; preserves recognised language. Tools (ANTLR) do this automatically; hand-written parsers may or may not.

sub_mechanisms.name: left_factoring
sub_mechanisms.definition: Transform A → α β | α γ into A → α (β | γ). Required for LL(1) when productions share a prefix.
sub_mechanisms.why: LL(1) needs the first token to uniquely identify the production. Shared prefixes prevent this. Factoring out the common prefix lets the parser commit AFTER reading α.

sub_mechanisms.name: LR_item
sub_mechanisms.definition: Grammar production with a marker indicating how much has been parsed. A → α • β means α has been read, β is yet to come.
sub_mechanisms.why: State in LR parser tracks 'which items are possible'. Item sets become DFA states. Computing them = the LR(0) automaton construction.

sub_mechanisms.name: LR0_automaton
sub_mechanisms.definition: DFA whose states are sets of LR items. Transitions on grammar symbols. Used as the LR parser's state machine.
sub_mechanisms.why: Item-set transitions encode 'after reading this symbol, what items are possible'. The DFA's states are the parser's states. Used to derive parsing tables.

sub_mechanisms.name: SLR_LALR_LR1
sub_mechanisms.definition: Variants of LR with increasing precision: SLR uses FOLLOW sets; LALR merges equivalent states (yacc default); LR(1) keeps separate states for precise lookahead.
sub_mechanisms.why: Trade-off table size vs grammar coverage. LR(1) is most precise but huge tables (~thousands of states). LALR is the common compromise — handles real grammars + reasonable table size.

sub_mechanisms.name: GLR_parser
sub_mechanisms.definition: Generalised LR. Handles arbitrary CFGs (including ambiguous) by maintaining multiple parse stacks simultaneously when shift-reduce conflicts arise.
sub_mechanisms.why: Lets grammars be written naturally without LR(1)-friendly transformations. Used in Bison's GLR mode, SDF, ASF+SDF. Worst case O(n³) (Earley/Tomita); linear for unambiguous grammars.

sub_mechanisms.name: operator_precedence_parsing
sub_mechanisms.definition: Special-case parser for expressions. Each operator has precedence + associativity. Pratt parsing uses recursive functions per precedence level.
sub_mechanisms.why: Expression grammars have many levels of precedence (1+2*3 = 1+(2*3)). General CFG parsing handles this but verbosely; precedence parsing is direct. Used in hand-written parsers for expression sub-grammar.

sub_mechanisms.name: pratt_parser
sub_mechanisms.definition: Top-down operator precedence parser. Each operator has 'binding power' (left + right). Recursion handles precedence; left/right binding powers handle associativity.
sub_mechanisms.why: Elegant for expression languages. Used in many hand-written compilers (TypeScript's parser, GCC's C++ frontend). Cleanly handles complex operator semantics; easy to extend.

sub_mechanisms.name: error_synchronisation
sub_mechanisms.definition: On parse error, skip input until reaching a recovery point (often a statement terminator like ; or }), then resume parsing.
sub_mechanisms.why: Allows reporting multiple errors per run. Quality depends on sync-point selection. Hand-tuned per language; recursive-descent parsers (Clang, Rust) have very good recovery via per-context sync sets.

derivation_rules.name: LL1_requires_FIRST_FOLLOW_disjoint
then: for every non-terminal A with productions A → α | β, FIRST(α) ∩ FIRST(β) = ∅, and if α can derive ε then FIRST(β) ∩ FOLLOW(A) = ∅
derivation_rules.why: These conditions ensure the parser can pick the right production with 1 token of lookahead. Violation = conflict in the LL(1) table. Standard test for LL(1) grammars.

derivation_rules.name: LR_handles_left_recursion_naturally
then: LR parsing handles it but LL requires elimination
derivation_rules.why: LR's shift-reduce builds left-recursive structures bottom-up. LL would infinite-loop trying to expand A → Aα. The structural reason yacc-style LR parsers are preferred for natural-looking grammars.

derivation_rules.name: shift_reduce_conflict_indicates_ambiguity
then: the grammar is ambiguous or LR-difficult
derivation_rules.why: Two valid parser actions at the same state means grammar permits multiple parses. Resolution: precedence rules, grammar rewriting, or default-to-shift. Ignoring conflicts produces wrong parse on ambiguous input.

derivation_rules.name: GLR_handles_ambiguity_at_runtime_cost
then: GLR's multiple stacks find all parses; cost is O(n³) worst-case
derivation_rules.why: Each conflict spawns a parallel stack. Most stacks die quickly; only valid parses survive. Linear time for unambiguous grammars; polynomial for ambiguous. Standard parser for natural language + grammars too complex for LALR.

derivation_rules.name: pratt_parser_natural_for_expressions
if: a language has rich operator precedence
then: Pratt parser's binding power scheme handles it naturally
derivation_rules.why: Operator's left + right binding power expresses precedence + associativity in two integers. Recursion is per-precedence-level. Less verbose than CFG with explicit precedence cascading. Used in TypeScript, V8, many production parsers.
